scenes.visual: Dark slate canvas (#0F172A), labelled 'schematic' in small corner tag. Establish the carried two-cell world filling 65% of frame height: upper curved membrane of a teal receptor cell (#2DD4BF) facing lower curved membrane of an amber ligand cell (#F59E0B) across a narrow extracellular cleft, membranes gently breathing. Bold white title 'When a Ligand Listens' centered over the cleft; fades out at 1.8 s while the two cells remain alive in place.

scenes.tts: When a receptor grips a ligand anchored in another cell's membrane, how can both cells get a message? Most signals we learn float freely across space. Once a free ligand leaves its home cell, that connection is gone.
scenes.caption: When a receptor grips a ligand anchored in another cell's membrane, how can both cells get a message? Most signals we learn float freely across space. Once a free ligand leaves its home cell, that connection is gone.
scenes.visual: Same two-cell world (teal cell above, amber cell below, schematic). On the left half, a free amber dot detaches from the lower cell, drifts across the cleft, and docks into a teal Y-shaped receptor block; a teal arrow pulses upward into the receptor cell, while the amber cell below stays dark with a broken dotted link. On the right half, a membrane-anchored amber block stays embedded in the lower bilayer, gripping a teal receptor; question marks pulse inside both cells. Labels >= 28 pt: 'Receptor cell', 'Ligand cell', 'Free ligand'.
scenes.narration: When a receptor grips a ligand anchored in another cell's membrane, how can both cells get a message? Most signals we learn float freely across space. Once a free ligand leaves its home cell, that connection is gone.

scenes.tts: Now tether that ligand in its own cell's membrane. When a receptor binds it, the receptor's cell gets the forward signal. The ligand's cell can get a reverse signal too. Why still call it a ligand? Those names only record which role biologists saw first.
scenes.caption: Now tether that ligand in its own cell's membrane. When a receptor binds it, the receptor's cell gets the forward signal. The ligand's cell can get a reverse signal too. Why still call it a ligand? Those names only record which role biologists saw first.
scenes.visual: The left free ligand fades out as the tethered amber ligand slides to center and locks with the teal receptor in a clasped handshake silhouette across the cleft. A bright teal arrow shoots upward into the upper cell, labelled 'Forward signal'. A bright amber arrow shoots downward into the lower cell, labelled 'Reverse signal'. Both arrows pulse continuously; brief label 'Bidirectional' spans the cleft while the two protein labels 'Receptor' (teal) and 'Ligand' (amber) gently swap highlight rings to show historical naming.
scenes.narration: Now tether that ligand in its own cell's membrane. When a receptor binds it, the receptor's cell gets the forward signal. The ligand's cell can get a reverse signal too. Why still call it a ligand? Those names only record which role biologists saw first.

scenes.tts: Sending a message inward takes two things. First, the ligand must stay attached to its own membrane. Second, it needs a path into the cytosol. A cytosolic tail is what you normally expect on a receptor. A membrane ligand can signal inward through a tail or partner.
scenes.caption: Sending a message inward takes two things. First, the ligand must stay attached to its own membrane. Second, it needs a path into the cytosol. A cytosolic tail is what you normally expect on a receptor. A membrane ligand can signal inward through a tail or partner.
scenes.visual: Camera zooms smoothly into the amber lower cell's membrane and cytosol (filling 70% of frame height). First, a highlight bracket pulses around the ligand's membrane anchor ('1. Stay anchored'). Second, the view splits gently across the lower membrane to preview two inward paths: on the left, an amber tail extending down into the cytosol ('Tail'); on the right, a violet partner block spanning the bilayer next to an outer-layer ligand ('Partner'). Particles drift slowly in the cytosol so the frame stays in continuous motion.
scenes.narration: Sending a message inward takes two things. First, the ligand must stay attached to its own membrane. Second, it needs a path into the cytosol. A cytosolic tail is what you normally expect on a receptor. A membrane ligand can signal inward through a tail or partner.

scenes.tts: Start with the tail route in B type ephrins. Each crosses the membrane once and ends in a short cytosolic tail. That tail has no kinase enzyme. Neither does the receptor's outer binding tip. Yet receptor contact puts phosphate onto tyrosines in that tail.
scenes.caption: Start with the tail route in B-type ephrins. Each crosses the membrane once and ends in a short cytosolic tail. That tail has no kinase enzyme. Neither does the receptor's outer binding tip. Yet receptor contact puts phosphate onto tyrosines in that tail.
scenes.visual: Focus solely on the amber B-type ephrin spanning the lower bilayer once, labelled 'Ephrin-B', with small open circles along its cytosolic tail marked 'Y'. A teal receptor outer tip ('EphB outer tip') drifts down from above and binds it; both the amber tail and the teal outer tip briefly flash a subtle 'No kinase' tag. Despite that, bright coral circles marked 'P' (#F43F5E) pop onto the tail's Y sites with a soft ripple and a '?'
scenes.narration: Start with the tail route in B-type ephrins. Each crosses the membrane once and ends in a short cytosolic tail. That tail has no kinase enzyme. Neither does the receptor's outer binding tip. Yet receptor contact puts phosphate onto tyrosines in that tail.

scenes.tts: How does phosphate appear with no kinase on either protein? Receptor binding pulls ephrins into dense clusters. Clustered tails draw sark family kinases from inside the ephrin's own cell. Those kinases add the phosphates. An adaptor then docks there and links the tail to actin.
scenes.caption: How does phosphate appear with no kinase on either protein? Receptor binding pulls ephrins into dense clusters. Clustered tails draw Src-family kinases from inside the ephrin's own cell. Those kinases add the phosphates. An adaptor then docks there and links the tail to actin.
scenes.visual: Three amber ephrin-B blocks slide laterally along the membrane into a tight cluster gripped by teal EphB tips above. Coral kinase blocks ('Src-family kinases', #F43F5E) glide up from the lower cytosol to the clustered tails and stamp glowing coral 'P' tags onto the tail tyrosines. A violet adaptor block ('Adaptor', #A78BFA) docks directly onto the coral 'P' tags and pulls on animated violet filament strands labelled 'Actin', bending the lower cytoskeleton smoothly.
scenes.narration: How does phosphate appear with no kinase on either protein? Receptor binding pulls ephrins into dense clusters. Clustered tails draw Src-family kinases from inside the ephrin's own cell. Those kinases add the phosphates. An adaptor then docks there and links the tail to actin.

scenes.tts: The same tail carries a second handle at its very tip, a P D Z binding site. After a delay, a phosphatase binds that end and strips the phosphates off. Other P D Z proteins also bind there, giving the tail a second route.
scenes.caption: The same tail carries a second handle at its very tip, a PDZ-binding site. After a delay, a phosphatase binds that end and strips the phosphates off. Other PDZ proteins also bind there, giving the tail a second route.
scenes.visual: Highlight the notched bottom tip of the amber ephrin-B tail, labelled 'PDZ site'. A small timer arc sweeps once; then a violet phosphatase block ('Phosphatase') glides onto the notched tip and sweeps upward, detaching the coral 'P' tags so they drift away and fade. Next to the cluster, another violet block ('PDZ partner') docks onto the notched tip and sends a separate violet signaling wave downward, showing two distinct routes from one tail.
scenes.narration: The same tail carries a second handle at its very tip, a PDZ-binding site. After a delay, a phosphatase binds that end and strips the phosphates off. Other PDZ proteins also bind there, giving the tail a second route.

scenes.tts: Now watch what happens when the tail disappears completely. An A type ephrin has no transmembrane segment and no cytosolic tail. A lipid called a G P I anchor holds it only in the outer membrane layer. When a receptor clusters it, how could a signal cross?
scenes.caption: Now watch what happens when the tail disappears completely. An A-type ephrin has no transmembrane segment and no cytosolic tail. A lipid called a GPI anchor holds it only in the outer membrane layer. When a receptor clusters it, how could a signal cross?
scenes.visual: The amber tail and membrane-spanning stalk retract and dissolve, morphing the protein into an amber outer block ('Ephrin-A') tethered solely to the upper slate leaflet by a short wavy lipid stem ('GPI anchor'). The bilayer's two leaflets are clearly separated so viewers see the anchor stops halfway and never touches the cytosol. Teal EphA tips cluster three ephrin-A blocks above; a bold white question card slides into the lower cytosol: 'No tail inside — how can a signal cross?'
scenes.narration: Now watch what happens when the tail disappears completely. An A-type ephrin has no transmembrane segment and no cytosolic tail. A lipid called a GPI anchor holds it only in the outer membrane layer. When a receptor clusters it, how could a signal cross?

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Keep the clustered amber ephrin-A blocks on the outer leaflet and the question card 'No tail inside — how can a signal cross?' in clear view. A subtle pulsing dashed arrow with a '?' breathes gently across the bilayer while a slim progress bar counts 4.5 s.

scenes.tts: It borrows a partner that reaches the inside, because a signal can only enter through something touching the cytosol. In some cells, a membrane spanning protein such as p seventy five pairs with the ephrin. In cholesterol rich patches, inner leaflet kinases like Fyn gather underneath. How a lipid patch alone crosses the bilayer remains unresolved.
scenes.caption: It borrows a partner that reaches the inside, because a signal can only enter through something touching the cytosol. In some cells, a membrane-spanning protein such as p75 pairs with the ephrin. In cholesterol-rich patches, inner-leaflet kinases like Fyn gather underneath. How a lipid patch alone crosses the bilayer remains unresolved.
scenes.visual: Question card fades smoothly. Beside the clustered amber ephrin-A, a violet membrane-spanning block ('p75 partner') slides in, touches ephrin-A in the bilayer, and sends a violet signal into the cytosol. Simultaneously, the bilayer under ephrin-A highlights as a warm patch ('Cholesterol-rich patch'); coral inner-leaflet kinase blocks ('Fyn') drift along the inner face into that patch. Keep a dashed '?' arrow between ephrin-A and Fyn labelled 'Not yet settled' so the visual matches the hedge.
scenes.narration: It borrows a partner that reaches the inside, because a signal can only enter through something touching the cytosol. In some cells, a membrane-spanning protein such as p75 pairs with the ephrin. In cholesterol-rich patches, inner-leaflet kinases like Fyn gather underneath. How a lipid patch alone crosses the bilayer remains unresolved.

scenes.tts: Different ligands solve the membrane barrier in different ways, yet the logic stays the same. Stay anchored at the surface, and couple receptor grip to an inward path. Whether through a tail or a partner, a membrane ligand can listen as well as speak.
scenes.caption: Different ligands solve the membrane barrier in different ways, yet the logic stays the same. Stay anchored at the surface, and couple receptor grip to an inward path. Whether through a tail or a partner, a membrane ligand can listen as well as speak.
scenes.visual: Camera pulls back smoothly to the full two-cell world (teal receptor cell above, amber ligand cell below) showing both solutions side by side along the contact zone: left, amber ephrin-B tail recruiting coral kinase and violet adaptor; right, amber ephrin-A with violet partner and coral Fyn. Teal upward and amber downward arrows glow together steadily across the cleft.
